extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, journalism students, newsroom researchers and newsroom practitioners (editors/reporters) interested in news values and news selection
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and applying criteria journalists use (explicit and implicit) to decide what is newsworthy in editorial conferences and everyday newsroom practice. Uses a Bourdieu-inspired field perspective to distinguish doxic (taken-for-granted) and orthodox/heterodox (arguable) news values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Most often described as current affairs, as new information. The closer to the media deadline the story is, the more timely it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness varies by medium: live television reports are among the most timely (reported as events happen), while print media have fixed deadlines requiring earlier cut-offs. Stories can be considered timely even a day or several days later if they still fit production constraints (e.g. 'stories on the shelf'). Use timeliness to prioritise stories near breaking events or deadlines; however, timeliness can be outweighed by other values such as exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected importance to the public as a whole or to the specific audience of a given media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly understood as either moderately important to many people or very important to a smaller, specific group. Relevance is more qualitative and harder to operationalise than timeliness; journalists invoke it to justify why an audience should care. It is used as a legitimisation resource during negotiations with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Closeness between public/audience and events (socially, geographically, culturally). The closer an event is to the audience, the more newsworthy it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cultural/geographical proximity influences coverage (e.g. stronger identification with New Orleans than with distant rural Kashmir). Identification can explain differential coverage of similar events in different places. Use assessment of audience proximity when judging emotional or practical resonance for the outlet's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting stories and angles that accentuate conflicts of interest between people, causes, organisations, parties or positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many political and institutional stories are packaged as conflicts ('Government says A, opposition says B'). The conflict criterion often determines framing and source selection. Editors will prioritise angles that foreground opposition, disagreement or stakes between actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The unusual, the spectacular, the extraordinary — stories with a sensational element are more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic heuristic: 'man-bites-dog' — the more spectacular or exceptional the event, the higher its news value. Sensational elements can elevate otherwise mundane events but may be deprioritised if they lack relevance or identification for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: A doxic (often tacit) news value: the degree to which a story is exclusive or ahead of competitors; stories not yet covered elsewhere gain newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often unspoken but highly influential in editorial decisions. Practiced via press review and awareness of what other media have or have not covered. Exclusivity can override other values (a less timely story may be chosen because it is exclusive; conversely, a timely story may be devalued if every competitor has it). Examples include using 'stories on the shelf' to fill slots only when exclusivity or originality is low elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard news versus soft news (orthodox/heterodox distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthodox (dominant) news values align with 'hard news' (politics, foreign affairs, economy) whereas heterodox (dominated/misrecognised) values align with 'soft news' (human interest, lifestyle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard news is institutionally privileged: it tends to receive more time and consideration in editorial conferences and is associated with prestige and resources. Soft news is frequently allocated with little discussion and often has lower prestige and pay. This distinction is also linked to newsroom hierarchies and gendered divisions of labour. Recognise how classifying a story as 'hard' or 'soft' affects its likelihood of being chosen and resourced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic gut feeling (ability to 'picture the story')
rubrics_metrics.description: A heuristic used by practitioners: 'Can I picture the story? Can I see the headline?' — if so, the story is believed to be newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a bodily, embodied sense ('part of your spinal cord') rather than a checklist. Operates as a fast decision-making tool within news habitus; helps triage many potential stories quickly. While powerful, it is tacit and may conceal structural biases; making it explicit can be a reflexive research task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press review / positioning in the news field
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily practice of surveying other media and news flows to map who is covering what and to decide what to treat; used to position one's outlet and stories relative to competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press review is a 'game of mirrors' — it both suggests subjects (because others are talking about them) and offers a way to distinguish angle or beat others. Journalists use press review to read positions in the field (which stories competitors have, which angles are taken), thereby informing exclusivity and positioning decisions. Over-reliance can render products similar; strategic use helps differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial capitals (professional experience, organisational position, prizes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agent-level resources (years of experience, formal organisational rank, specialist beats, journalistic prizes) that confer prestige and influence which proposals are accepted or discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different distributions of editorial capital shape whose ideas carry weight: a senior correspondent's suggestion (high internal prestige) may be accepted without discussion, while an intern's identical suggestion will be treated differently. Editorial capital structures the practical application of news criteria and affects allocation of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: News habitus / professional habitus
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical mastery or bodily disposition for the news game shared by practitioners (news habitus), differentiated across roles (editorial habitus, reporter habitus, intern habitus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News habitus explains fast, routinised decision-making and why explicit discussion is limited: practitioners 'feel' newsworthiness. Habitus is relational and depends on position within the social space; it accounts for consistent patterns in how news criteria are applied and for variations across subfields or beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using news criteria as legitimisation or negotiation resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The five institutionalised news criteria (timeliness, relevance, identification, conflict, sensation) are available as discursive tools to justify story choices when negotiating with editors or colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although these criteria are 'known by heart', they are rarely articulated in everyday work and instead reside 'in the back of your head'. They become explicit when journalists need to legitimise a choice (e.g. 'Why are we doing this story?'). Be aware that invoking these criteria can be strategic and contingent on the proposer's editorial capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning the news (assessing newsworthiness relationally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness is not intrinsic to an event but constructed by positioning: considering how a story relates to other stories, which outlets have it, and who proposes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a field-perspective: ask which stories are on the agenda; how is the journalist or outlet positioned relative to others; what is the distribution of capital shaping this decision. This relational assessment integrates press review, exclusivity, editorial capital and habitus into a single evaluative move.
